stem: A patient with chronic plaque psoriasis presents with plaques covering 15% of body surface area. He has been on topical therapy for several weeks with minimal improvement. What is the next best step in management?
keywords: Plaques covering 15% of body surface area (BSA) – Indicates moderate psoriasis, signaling that topical therapy alone is insufficient.
Minimal improvement with topical therapy – Shows treatment-refractory disease, pointing toward the need for phototherapy or systemic therapy.
These two keywords are sufficient to identify the correct next step (Option E).

E.title: Start phototherapy or systemic therapy
E.body:
When psoriasis involves >10% of the Body Surface Area (BSA) or is recalcitrant to topicals, it is classified as moderate-to-severe. The next line of treatment involves Narrowband UVB phototherapy or systemic agents (like Methotrexate, Cyclosporine, or Biologics).
In dermatology, we follow a "stepped" approach to psoriasis. When the disease covers more than 10% of the body, it is physically and psychologically burdensome.
Phototherapy (NB-UVB): Uses specific wavelengths of light to slow down the rapid growth of skin cells and suppress the overactive immune response in the skin. It is often the preferred next step because it lacks the internal organ side effects of oral medications.
Systemic Therapy: If phototherapy is unavailable or ineffective, systemic medications are used. These include traditional orals (Methotrexate) or newer Biologics (e.g., Adalimumab, Ustekinumab), which target specific inflammatory cytokines like TNF-alpha or IL-17.
These treatments target the immune-mediated pathophysiology of psoriasis, suppressing T-cell activation and keratinocyte hyperproliferation, leading to plaque improvement.

A.title: Continue topical therapy only
A.body: Incorrect because the patient has moderate psoriasis (>10% BSA) and topical therapy alone is insufficient. Continuing the same treatment will not achieve adequate disease control.

B.title: Add oral antihistamines
B.body: Antihistamines are not disease-modifying in psoriasis; they only help with pruritus, which is symptomatic relief and does not treat plaques.

C.title: Use antibiotics
C.body: Psoriasis is not an infectious disease; antibiotics have no role unless there is a secondary bacterial infection, which is not mentioned here.

D.title: Cosmetic camouflage
D.body: Cosmetic camouflage addresses appearance only and does not treat the underlying disease, so it is not appropriate for moderate-to-severe psoriasis requiring systemic control.

keyConcept:
Moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (BSA >10%) with poor response to topicals requires phototherapy or systemic therapy.
Topicals are first-line for mild disease, but immune-modulating therapy is needed for larger BSA or refractory disease.
Symptomatic treatments (antihistamines, camouflage) or antibiotics do not alter disease progression.

Indicates need for:systemic therapy or phototherapy

featureTable.description: Phototherapy (narrowband UVB), systemic agents (methotrexate, acitretin, biologics)
featureTable.clinicalImportance: Choice depends on:comorbidities, severity, patient preference, and guideline recommendations

differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Usually less well-demarcated, oozing/crusting, history of atopy

differentialDiagnosisTable.distinguishingFeatures: Greasy, yellowish scales, often on scalp, face, chest
differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Greasy scales, involvement of seborrheic areas, less sharply demarcated
Positive KOH prep, responds to antifungals

differentialDiagnosisTable.distinguishingFeatures: Follicular papules with orange-red plaques, palmoplantar keratoderma
differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Island of sparing pattern, widespread involvement

differentialDiagnosisTable.distinguishingFeatures: Purple, polygonal, flat-topped papules, often on wrists/ankles

differentialDiagnosisTable.keyDifferences: Photosensitivity, lab markers positive, chronic scarring

diagram.name: Psoriasis – Chronic Plaque Psoriasis: Moderate Disease Management
diagram.caption: This diagram illustrates the management approach for moderate chronic plaque psoriasis, defined by 10–30% body surface area involvement with poor response to topical therapy. It emphasizes treatment escalation to phototherapy (narrowband UVB) or systemic agents (e.g., methotrexate, acitretin, biologics), guided by disease severity, comorbidities, patient preference, and clinical guidelines.
